# Assembly line and mass production (`assembly_line`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/manufacturing.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Tools, machines & manufacturing (`manufacturing`)
- Deps: needs interchangeable_parts, division_of_labour; helped by machine_tools, belt_drive, dynamo_electric_motor
- Core idea: Break the making of a product into short steps, place the machines and workers in the order of the steps, and move the work past them at a fixed pace on a chain or belt, so that nobody walks, fetches or waits. Parts must fit without adjustment, or the line stops at the first bad one. Every station must take the same time, so long jobs are split or doubled. At Ford's Highland Park works the time to assemble a chassis fell from about twelve and a half man-hours to about one and a half between 1913 and 1914. The price is monotony: labour turnover reached 370 % in 1913 until wages were doubled to five dollars a day.
- Pitfalls:
  - A line fed with parts that need fitting
  - One slow station holds up all the others; the line must be balanced
  - Ignoring the workers: mass quitting, absenteeism and sabotage
  - A product made in numbers too small to pay for the special machines
- History: china: 3rd c. BC – Qin workshops make weapons and the terracotta army from standard modules; later the Jingdezhen porcelain works pass each piece through dozens of hands; europe: 15th–16th c. – the Venice Arsenal fits out galleys in sequence along a canal; 1803–1805 Portsmouth block mills: 45 machines, ten men doing the work of 110; americas: 1860s – overhead 'disassembly' lines in Cincinnati and Chicago meat packing; 1901 Olds's staged assembly; 1913 moving line at Ford's Highland Park plant
- Read:
  - David A. Hounshell, From the American System to Mass Production, 1800–1932 (1984)
  - Henry Ford with Samuel Crowther, My Life and Work (1922)
